```{r}
#| label: setup
#| include: false

options(width = 90)
options(cli.unicode = FALSE)
pkg_root <- if (file.exists("DESCRIPTION")) {
  "."
} else if (file.exists("../DESCRIPTION")) {
  ".."
} else {
  NA_character_
}
if (!is.na(pkg_root) && requireNamespace("pkgload", quietly = TRUE)) {
  pkgload::load_all(pkg_root, quiet = TRUE)
}
default_output_hook <- knitr::knit_hooks$get("output")
knitr::knit_hooks$set(
  output = function(x, options) {
    x <- gsub(
      "Database:(\\s+)[^\\r\\n]+[.]duckdb",
      "Database:\\1<temporary DuckDB path>",
      x,
      perl = TRUE
    )
    x <- gsub("[ \t]+(?=\n)", "", x, perl = TRUE)
    default_output_hook(x, options)
  }
)

# A sealed point-in-time snapshot that an adapter or a colleague built
# earlier. The next article shows how such a snapshot is prepared.
ids <- sprintf("DEMO_%02d", 1:8)
pit <- ledgr::ledgr_sim_pit_inputs(ids, from = "2020-01-01", to = "2020-12-31", seed = 7L)
facts <- ledgr::ledgr_facts(
  ledgr::ledgr_facts_sessions(pit$sessions, venue_id = "DEMO_VENUE",
                              knowledge = "evidenced", timezone = "UTC"),
  ledgr::ledgr_facts_membership_snapshots(pit$membership, universe_id = "DEMO_UNIVERSE",
                                          complete = TRUE, knowledge = "evidenced"),
  ledgr::ledgr_facts_trading_status(pit$trading_status, knowledge = "evidenced"),
  ledgr::ledgr_facts_lifetime(pit$lifetime, knowledge = "evidenced"),
  ledgr::ledgr_facts_equity_corporate_actions(pit$corporate_actions)
)
snapshot_path <- file.path(tempdir(), "causal-history-demo.duckdb")
if (file.exists(snapshot_path)) unlink(snapshot_path)
built <- ledgr::ledgr_snapshot_from_df(
  pit$bars, instruments_df = pit$instruments, facts = facts,
  db_path = snapshot_path, snapshot_id = "history_demo",
  price_basis = "split_adjusted"
)
ledgr::ledgr_snapshot_close(built)
```

A strategy sees one pulse at a time, but most estimators need a window of
past values: a covariance matrix, a trailing volatility, a momentum score.
`ledgr_history_frame()` returns that window from inside the strategy, already
aligned to the venue's sessions and cut off at the pulse. Every value in it
was observed at or before the pulse, and every fact behind it was knowable
then.

This article starts from a snapshot that already exists, runs it once, and
then reads history the way a strategy would: defaults first, then the
explicit choices, then the evidence that explains each cell. It ends with one
portfolio estimate that goes from history to targets without rebuilding any
timestamp or instrument name by hand.

## Open A Snapshot And Run It

Someone has already sealed a point-in-time snapshot of eight synthetic
instruments over 2020. In this article it was built in a setup step that is
not shown, from the inputs `ledgr_sim_pit_inputs()` returns (kept as `pit`),
and written to the DuckDB file whose path is `snapshot_path`. The next
article, on point-in-time inputs, shows that preparation step by step.
Opening the file, declaring an experiment and running it takes three calls.

```{r}
#| label: hello-world
#| message: false

library(ledgr)

snapshot <- ledgr_snapshot_open(snapshot_path)

momentum <- function(ctx, params) {
  ctx |>
    ledgr_signal_return(params$lookback) |>
    ledgr_select_top_n(params$n, partial = "allow") |>
    ledgr_weight_equal() |>
    ledgr_target_rebalance(ctx, equity_fraction = 0.95)
}

exp <- ledgr_experiment(
  snapshot,
  momentum,
  features = list(ledgr_ind_returns(20L)),
  universe = ledgr_universe_members("DEMO_UNIVERSE"),
  cost_model = ledgr_cost_zero()
)

bt <- exp |> ledgr_run(params = list(lookback = 20L, n = 3L), run_id = "hello-history")
bt
```

The snapshot already declares a venue calendar, a changing universe,
trading halts, a delisting and a dividend, so the experiment reads them
without further declarations. The inputs it was built from are in `pit`;
`pit$cases` lists where each of those teaching cases sits. The rest of this
article looks inside single decisions of experiments like this one.

## Read History From Inside A Strategy

`ledgr_pulse_snapshot()` builds the context a run would hand to its strategy
at one session, without running anything. That makes it the easiest place to
try a history read.

```{r}
#| label: default-read

ctx <- ledgr_pulse_snapshot(exp, ts_utc = as.Date("2020-06-30"),
                            params = list(lookback = 20L, n = 3L))
closes <- ctx |> ledgr_history_frame(bar = "close", lookback = Inf)
closes
```

The defaults are the ones most estimators want, but the history width is
always explicit:

- `lookback = Inf` returns every expected venue session from the start of the
  data up to the pulse. A finite `lookback` returns the last sessions of that
  same history, so a shorter read is never computed differently.
- `instruments = "admissible"` returns the instruments the strategy may
  target at this pulse.
- `min_observations = NULL` requires one finite treated value for every
  requested session. Set a smaller integer when the estimator can work with
  incomplete columns.
- `min_instruments = 1L` records how many included instruments the strategy
  needs before it is ready. It does not remove another column.
- `layout = "wide"` returns one row per session, `ts_utc` first, then one
  column per instrument.

## Read A Matrix Directly

Estimators usually want a numeric matrix, so the context form of
`ledgr_history_matrix()` reads one directly. It uses the same causal plan as
the frame reader, keeps the session stamps and instrument IDs as dimension
names, and does not build a data frame first. The one-argument form remains an
adapter when a frame is useful for inspection.

```{r}
#| label: matrix

returns <- ctx |>
  ledgr_history_matrix(feature = "return_20", lookback = 5L)
returns

return_frame <- ctx |>
  ledgr_history_frame(feature = "return_20", lookback = 5L)
identical(as.matrix(returns), as.matrix(ledgr_history_matrix(return_frame)))
```

`ledgr_history_info()` returns what the result records about itself: its
source, cutoff, window, how many sessions it holds and which requested
instruments it includes or left out.

```{r}
#| label: info

ledgr_history_info(returns)
```

`Used before window: yes` says that some returned value depends on sessions
before the returned window: each 20-session return in these five rows was
computed from closes up to 20 sessions earlier.

## Choose The Instruments And The Required Observations

The defaults can be replaced one at a time. `instruments = "decision_axis"`
adds held nonmembers and members the strategy may not trade now. Here that
is `DEMO_01`, still a member of the universe but delisted on 14 January, so it
is not admissible at the cutoff. `min_observations` leaves an instrument out
of the estimate when it has too few finite treated values, and records why.
Finite input-carried and output-carried values count because they are values
the declared history policy admitted.

```{r}
#| label: explicit-choices

window <- ctx |>
  ledgr_history_frame(bar = "close", lookback = 120L,
                      instruments = "decision_axis",
                      min_observations = 100L)
info <- ledgr_history_info(window)
info
info$selection[, c("instrument_id", "requested", "included", "exclusion_reason")]
```

`structural_exclusion` means the window crosses a lifetime or terminal
barrier, here `DEMO_01`'s delisting, rather than a missing observation
(`insufficient_observations`) or a carry that ran out (`carry_expired`).
Leaving an instrument out of an estimate is an estimation choice only. It
creates no target, no zero target and no order.

The long layout returns one row per session and instrument, with the evidence
for each cell next to its value.

```{r}
#| label: long-layout

long <- ctx |> ledgr_history_frame(bar = "close", lookback = 3L, layout = "long")
as.data.frame(long)[, c("ts_utc", "instrument_id", "value", "observed",
                        "input_carried", "missing_reason")]
```

## Is The Requested Panel Ready?

The history request records both requirements. `min_observations` filters each
instrument independently; `min_instruments` asks how many included instruments
the strategy needs. `ledgr_passed_warmup()` reads the resulting readiness bit
without rescanning the matrix.

```{r}
#| label: sufficiency

recent <- ctx |>
  ledgr_history_frame(feature = "return_20", lookback = 60L,
                      min_instruments = 3L)
ledgr_passed_warmup(recent)

early <- ledgr_pulse_snapshot(exp, ts_utc = as.Date("2020-01-15"),
                              params = list(lookback = 20L, n = 3L))
early_returns <- early |>
  ledgr_history_frame(feature = "return_20", lookback = 60L,
                      min_instruments = 3L)
ledgr_passed_warmup(early_returns)
```

In January there are not yet 60 finite returned observations per instrument,
so the answer is `FALSE`. For history objects the familiar warm-up helper
means that the recorded panel requirements passed; it does not rescan cells.
Feature-cell readiness remains separate evidence, described next.

## Feature History And Indicator Classes

Every indicator belongs to one of two history classes. A bounded indicator,
such as a 20-session return or a simple moving average, depends only on its
last `requires_bars` expected sessions. A history-dependent indicator, such
as TTR's recursive exponential moving average, depends on everything before
it and starts again after a gap it cannot bridge. Printing an indicator shows
its class and where the class comes from.

```{r}
#| label: indicator-classes

ledgr_ind_sma(20)
ledgr_ind_ttr("EMA", input = "close", n = 10)
```

Feature cells carry their own evidence. `ready` turns `TRUE` once a cell has
enough admitted sessions behind it, `calculation_valid` once it is ready and
finite, and `missing_reason` says why any other cell has no usable value.

```{r}
#| label: feature-evidence

warm <- ctx |>
  ledgr_history_frame(feature = "return_20", lookback = Inf,
                      instruments = "DEMO_05", layout = "long")
as.data.frame(warm)[19:22, c("ts_utc", "value", "ready", "calculation_valid",
                             "missing_reason")]
```

The first 20 cells are `not_ready`: a 20-session return needs 21 closes.

## Carried Prices Are Disclosed

By default the experiment's history policy carries a missing open, high, low
or close forward for at most five expected sessions; volume never carries.
A carried cell says so, with its source session and age.

```{r}
#| label: carry

pit$cases
gap <- pit$cases[pit$cases$type == "missing_observation", ]
open_days <- as.Date(pit$sessions$session_date[pit$sessions$status == "open"])
after_gap <- open_days[match(as.Date(gap$date), open_days) + 2L]
gap_ctx <- ledgr_pulse_snapshot(exp, ts_utc = after_gap,
                                params = list(lookback = 20L, n = 3L))
carried <- gap_ctx |>
  ledgr_history_frame(bar = "close", lookback = 4L,
                      instruments = gap$instrument_id, layout = "long")
as.data.frame(carried)[, c("ts_utc", "value", "observed", "input_carried",
                           "source_ts_utc", "carry_age_sessions")]
```

The selection table counts how much of each instrument's window was carried:

```{r}
#| label: carried-share

ledgr_history_info(carried)$selection[, c("instrument_id", "required_input_count",
                                          "carried_input_count",
                                          "carried_input_share")]
```

`ledgr_history_policy(price_carry = NULL)` turns input carry off, so a missing
close stays missing.

## Read Return Features, Not Differences Of Carried Closes

A carried close repeats the previous close, so a return computed by
differencing the close history is exactly zero on the missing session, and
the next session carries the whole two-session move as if it were one day.
Neither number is an observed daily return. Return and volatility features
never consume a carried price: the cell on the missing session is missing
with the reason `carried_input_excluded`, the next one is `not_ready` while
the return restarts, and the first return computed from two observed closes
follows.

```{r}
#| label: returns-not-diff

with_return <- ledgr_experiment(
  snapshot, momentum,
  features = list(ledgr_ind_returns(1L)),
  universe = ledgr_universe_members("DEMO_UNIVERSE"),
  cost_model = ledgr_cost_zero()
)
gap_ctx1 <- ledgr_pulse_snapshot(with_return, ts_utc = after_gap,
                                 params = list(lookback = 1L, n = 3L))
close_window <- gap_ctx1 |>
  ledgr_history_frame(bar = "close", lookback = 4L, instruments = gap$instrument_id)
closes <- ledgr_history_matrix(close_window)[, 1]
diff(closes) / head(closes, -1)

return_cells <- gap_ctx1 |>
  ledgr_history_frame(feature = "return_1", lookback = 3L,
                      instruments = gap$instrument_id, layout = "long")
as.data.frame(return_cells)[, c("ts_utc", "value", "missing_reason")]
```

## From History To Targets

This is the whole estimation flow in one strategy: read a window of daily
returns, turn a covariance estimate into weights with a small stand-in
solver, name the solver's output through the history result, and turn the
weights into targets. The solver is defined inside the strategy, because
preflight refuses a strategy that depends on a function from the calling
session.

The stand-in is not a long-only minimum-variance solver. It solves the
unconstrained problem, sets negative weights to zero and rescales the rest,
which in general is not the long-only optimum.
`vignette("minimum-variance", package = "ledgr")` builds the constrained
strategy with a quadratic-programming solver, screens and decision dates.

```{r}
#| label: portfolio

estimate <- function(ctx, params) {
  # A stand-in solver, not a long-only minimum-variance solver: unconstrained
  # weights with negatives set to zero. It returns an unnamed vector in the
  # column order of its input.
  clipped_weights <- function(sigma) {
    w <- solve(sigma + diag(1e-6, ncol(sigma)), rep(1, ncol(sigma)))
    w <- pmax(as.vector(w), 0)
    w / sum(w)
  }
  returns <- ctx |>
    ledgr_history_matrix(feature = "return_1", lookback = params$lookback,
                         min_instruments = 3L)
  if (!ledgr_passed_warmup(returns)) {
    return(ctx$hold())
  }
  w <- clipped_weights(stats::cov(returns))
  held <- ctx$universe[ctx$vec$position != 0]
  keep <- intersect(ledgr_history_info(returns)$excluded_ids, held)
  if (!isTRUE(params$keep)) keep <- character()
  w |>
    ledgr_align_weights(returns) |>
    ledgr_target_rebalance(ctx, equity_fraction = 0.95, keep = keep)
}

estimating <- ledgr_experiment(
  snapshot, estimate,
  features = list(ledgr_ind_returns(1L)),
  universe = ledgr_universe_members("DEMO_UNIVERSE"),
  cost_model = ledgr_cost_zero()
)
```

At one pulse, the strategy returns a full target, a share quantity for
every instrument; `c()` prints all of them:

```{r}
#| label: portfolio-decision

june <- ledgr_pulse_snapshot(estimating, ts_utc = as.Date("2020-06-30"),
                             params = list(lookback = 40L, keep = TRUE))
c(estimate(june, list(lookback = 40L, keep = TRUE)))
```

`ledgr_align_weights()` reads the unnamed solver output in the order of the
history result's included instruments and refuses a vector of the wrong
length, so no column name is rebuilt by hand.

Two separate choices are at work. Estimation exclusion decides which
instruments enter the covariance estimate. Execution intent decides what
happens to each position. `ledgr_target_rebalance()` targets every eligible
instrument without a weight to zero, so an instrument the estimate dropped
would be sold. Passing the dropped instruments that are held in `keep`
preserves those positions instead. The excluded IDs come from
`ledgr_history_info()`; the held ones from the context. A held instrument
that is no longer admissible is not requested under the default selector, so
it never appears among the excluded IDs; `ledgr_target_rebalance()` already
preserves such holdings. (The `params$keep` switch exists only so the next
example can show both choices.)

To see `keep` act, run the estimate with a three-session window, so that it
starts trading in early January and `DEMO_04`'s missing close on 9 January
falls inside the window while the position is held. Once with `keep` and
once without:

```{r}
#| label: portfolio-run

estimated <- estimating |>
  ledgr_run(params = list(lookback = 3L, keep = TRUE), run_id = "history-estimate")
without_keep <- estimating |>
  ledgr_run(params = list(lookback = 3L, keep = FALSE), run_id = "history-estimate-no-keep")
demo_04_fills <- function(bt) {
  fills <- as.data.frame(ledgr_results(bt, "fills"))
  fills[fills$instrument_id == "DEMO_04" &
          fills$ts_utc < as.POSIXct("2020-01-17", tz = "UTC"),
        c("ts_utc", "side", "qty")]
}
demo_04_fills(estimated)
demo_04_fills(without_keep)
```

Both runs buy 357 shares of `DEMO_04` on 8 January. On 9 January its close
is missing, so the estimates of the next sessions leave it out. With `keep`
the position stays until the estimate itself reduces it on 16 January.
Without `keep` the rebalance targets it to zero and sells all 357 shares at
the next open, on 10 January, then buys some back on 16 January once the
instrument is in the estimate again.

```{r}
#| label: portfolio-summary

estimated
```

## When A Fact Arrives Late

Facts can become known after the sessions they describe. A lifetime fact may
say an instrument was inactive for two sessions, but arrive only on the
third. The two kinds of history treat that differently:

- bar history is restated with what is known at the cutoff, so a read after
  the fact arrives marks those sessions as inactive;
- feature history is a vintage view, so each feature cell keeps the value and
  the evidence it had at its own pulse. The late fact changes feature cells
  only from the pulse at which it became known.

```{r}
#| label: late-fact

days <- as.Date("2021-01-04") + c(0:4, 7:9)
close_at <- function(d) as.POSIXct(paste(d, "21:00:00"), tz = "UTC")
open_at <- function(d) as.POSIXct(paste(d, "14:30:00"), tz = "UTC")
late_bars <- data.frame(
  instrument_id = rep(c("AAA", "DDD"), each = 8L),
  ts_utc = rep(close_at(days), 2L),
  close = c(11:18, 41, 43, 46, 50, 55, 61, 68, 76)
)
late_bars$open <- late_bars$high <- late_bars$low <- late_bars$close
late_bars$volume <- 100
calendar <- seq(min(days), max(days), by = "day")
is_open <- calendar %in% days
late_members <- data.frame(effective_from = close_at(days[[1L]] - 1),
                           knowledge_time = close_at(days[[1L]] - 1))
late_members$members <- I(list(c("AAA", "DDD")))
late_facts <- ledgr_facts(
  ledgr_facts_sessions(data.frame(
    session_date = calendar, status = ifelse(is_open, "open", "closed"),
    session_open = ifelse(is_open, "14:30:00", NA),
    session_close = ifelse(is_open, "21:00:00", NA)
  ), venue_id = "LATE_VENUE", knowledge = "assume_effective"),
  ledgr_facts_membership_snapshots(late_members, universe_id = "late",
                                   complete = TRUE, knowledge = "assume_effective"),
  ledgr_facts_lifetime(data.frame(
    instrument_id = "DDD",
    effective_from = open_at(days[[5L]]),
    effective_to = open_at(days[[7L]]),
    knowledge_time = open_at(days[[7L]]),
    assertion = "known_inactive",
    terminal_event = NA_character_
  ))
)
late_snapshot <- ledgr_snapshot_from_df(
  late_bars, data.frame(instrument_id = c("AAA", "DDD")),
  db_path = file.path(tempdir(), "late-fact.duckdb"),
  snapshot_id = "late_fact", facts = late_facts, price_basis = "split_adjusted"
)
late_exp <- ledgr_experiment(
  late_snapshot, function(ctx, params) {
    ctx$hold()
  },
  features = ledgr_feature_map(sma = ledgr_ind_sma(2)),
  universe = ledgr_universe_members("late"),
  cost_model = ledgr_cost_zero()
)
read_ddd <- function(day, ...) {
  ctx <- ledgr_pulse_snapshot(late_exp, ts_utc = day)
  on.exit(close(ctx))
  out <- ctx |>
    ledgr_history_frame(..., lookback = Inf,
                        instruments = "DDD", min_observations = 0L,
                        layout = "long")
  as.data.frame(out)[5:6, c("ts_utc", "value", "expected", "missing_reason")]
}
read_ddd(days[[6L]], bar = "close")
read_ddd(days[[7L]], bar = "close")
read_ddd(days[[7L]], feature = "sma")
```

Read at the sixth session, both sessions are ordinary. Read at the seventh,
after the fact is known, the bar history marks them as prints from an
inactive interval, while the moving-average cells keep the values they were
computed with at the time.

## Walk-Forward Windows Read One History

A walk-forward test window does not start its history at the window start.
Every run, sweep candidate and window reads the same history from the start
of the data, so a feature or a history read at the first pulse of a test
window sees everything before the window, as it would inside one long run.

To see what a test window reads, this strategy holds as many shares of one
instrument as its history read has sessions. Each test window below starts
flat (`opening_state_policy = "flat_test_state"`), so the first fill of a
window is the number of sessions the strategy saw at that window's first
pulse.

```{r}
#| label: walk-forward

count_history <- function(ctx, params) {
  sessions <- nrow(ledgr_history_frame(ctx, bar = "close", lookback = Inf))
  target <- ctx$hold()
  target[[params$instrument]] <- sessions
  target
}
counting <- ledgr_experiment(
  snapshot, count_history,
  universe = ledgr_universe_members("DEMO_UNIVERSE"),
  cost_model = ledgr_cost_zero()
)
folds <- ledgr_folds_rolling(start = "2020-01-01", end = "2021-01-01",
                             train_window = "6 months", test_window = "3 months")
wf <- ledgr_walk_forward(
  counting, ledgr_strategy_grid(instrument = "DEMO_05"), folds,
  selection_rule = ledgr_rule_argmax("sharpe_ratio"), seed = 1L,
  opening_state_policy = "flat_test_state"
)
wf$folds[, c("fold_seq", "test_start_utc", "status")]
first_fills <- lapply(wf$test_runs, function(bt) {
  head(as.data.frame(ledgr_results(bt, "fills"))[, c("ts_utc", "instrument_id", "qty")], 1)
})
do.call(rbind, first_fills)
```

Each fill happens at the next open after the decision. At the first pulse
of the first test window, 1 July, the strategy read 130 sessions: every
session since 1 January, not just the window. At the first pulse of the
second window, 1 October, it read 196, again from 1 January. Neither window
starts its history at its own start.

Outside this demonstration, the default `opening_state_policy = "carry_test_state"` carries the
portfolio across window boundaries, so consecutive test windows form one
continuous economic chain.

## Read A Finite Lookback

`lookback = Inf` is convenient for exploring, but a strategy that reads the
whole history at every pulse allocates in proportion to everything seen so
far, and the total work over a run grows with the square of its length. Read
the window your estimator needs.

```{r}
#| label: finite-lookback

full <- ctx |> ledgr_history_frame(feature = "return_20", lookback = Inf)
last_60 <- ctx |> ledgr_history_frame(feature = "return_20", lookback = 60L)
vapply(list(full = full, last_60 = last_60),
       function(x) format(utils::object.size(x), units = "Kb"), character(1))
```

Both reads end at the same pulse and agree on every session they share; the
first grows with every pulse of a run, the second does not.

## What ledgr Guarantees

ledgr guarantees that its own history, feature and fact readers return only
data known at the decision time. Strategy code outside them is the author's
responsibility. `ledgr_strategy_preflight()` helps with a best-effort static
check: it refuses code that reaches private context internals, non-exported
ledgr objects or environment-inspecting functions, which is how a strategy
could otherwise reach prepared data from later sessions.

```{r}
#| label: preflight

peeking <- function(ctx, params) {
  future <- ctx$.history
  ctx$hold()
}
ledgr_strategy_preflight(peeking)
```

Preflight is not a sandbox. R gives a strategy no private memory, so code that
deliberately works around the check, for example by reading a file of future
prices, is outside what ledgr can guarantee.

invisible(lapply(list(ctx, early, gap_ctx, gap_ctx1, june), close))
